extracted.intended_audience: agency officials, administrative lawyers, and others implementing or reviewing APA rulemaking and adjudication procedures
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance on how agencies must conduct rulemaking (formal and informal), publish procedures, handle petitions, set effective dates, and conduct adjudications under the Administrative Procedure Act. Emphasizes when formal on-the-record procedures (sections 5,7,8) apply and enumerates exemptions and notice requirements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Informal rulemaking may rely on agency file and expertise
rubrics_metrics.description: Except in formal rule making governed by sections 7 and 8, an agency is free to formulate rules upon the basis of materials in its file and the knowledge and experience of the agency, in addition to the materials adduced in public rule making proceedings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Agencies need not base informal rules exclusively on a public 'record' created during proceedings; internal materials and agency expertise are permissible bases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Section 4(b) — concise general statement of basis and purpose
rubrics_metrics.description: Upon completion of public rulemaking proceedings 'after consideration of all relevant matter presented, the agency shall incorporate in any rules adopted a concise general statement of their basis and purpose'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The statement should be 'concise' and 'general'. It is intended to advise the public of the general basis and purpose; findings of fact and conclusions of law or an elaborate analysis are not required. Courts and the public will use these statements in interpreting rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: When statute requires 'on the record after opportunity for an agency hearing', formal rulemaking (sections 7 and 8) applies
rubrics_metrics.description: Where rules are required by statute to be made on the record after opportunity for an agency hearing, the requirements of sections 7 and 8 shall apply in place of the informal procedures of section 4.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If another statute mandates rulemaking 'on the record', public rulemaking proceedings must consist of a hearing and decision in accordance with sections 7 and 8 (formal procedures). Sections 7 and 8 apply only to proceedings initiated after their effective date.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statutes requiring decision on the record (FDCA example)
rubrics_metrics.description: Certain statutes (e.g., the Federal Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act) require agency orders to be based only on substantial evidence of record at the hearing and to set forth detailed findings of fact.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where statute explicitly requires decision 'on the record' and substantial-evidence review, agencies must conduct hearings and make findings as part of the order; on judicial review, findings supported by substantial evidence are conclusive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rate-setting statutes imply record-based decision and judicial-review transcript filing
rubrics_metrics.description: Statutes authorizing agencies to prescribe future rates after opportunity for hearing typically are construed (by agencies and courts) to require that such rates be established on the basis of the evidentiary record made in the hearing and that a transcript of the record be filed on review.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judicial-review provisions (e.g., requirement to file transcript and defer to findings supported by substantial evidence) can supply the inference that decisions must be made 'on the record'. Examples include the Natural Gas Act and rate orders under the Urgent Deficiencies Act.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hearing-required statutes that do not mandate decision 'on the record' (Federal Seed Act example)
rubrics_metrics.description: Some statutes require agencies to hold hearings prior to promulgating rules but contain no language from which the further requirement of decision 'on the record' can be inferred; such hearings may be intended merely to permit interested persons to express their views.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Legislative history suggests Congress did not intend sections 7 and 8 to apply where the statutory purpose was only to provide an opportunity for expression of views (as opposed to formal adjudicatory fact‑finding).

rubrics_metrics.name: Publish rulemaking procedures under section 3(a)(2)
rubrics_metrics.description: Each agency should publish under section 3(a)(2) the procedures, formal and informal, pursuant to which the public may participate in the formulation of its rules.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Statements of informal procedures may be specific or general. If procedures vary by type of rule, an agency may state generally that proposed substantive rules will be adopted after allowing public participation by written data, oral testimony, etc., with the method specified in the Federal Register notice for each case.

rubrics_metrics.name: Section 4(c) — 30-day publication/service requirement for substantive rules
rubrics_metrics.description: The required publication or service of any substantive rule (other than exemptions, interpretative rules, and statements of policy) shall be made not less than thirty days prior to the effective date thereof except as otherwise provided by the agency upon good cause found and published with the rule.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Purpose is to afford persons affected reasonable time to prepare for the effective date or take other action. Applies to substantive rules published in the Federal Register or served on named persons when substantive. Does not relate back to the general notice of proposed rulemaking under section 4(a).

rubrics_metrics.name: Exceptions to 30-day requirement and 'good cause' shortening
rubrics_metrics.description: Rules granting or recognizing exemption or relieving restriction, interpretative rules and statements of policy are excepted from the thirty-day requirement; the period may be shortened by an agency 'upon good cause found and published with the rule'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Good cause includes cases where public interest requires immediate action or when affected persons request a shorter effective period. If issued immediately for good cause, rule becomes effective as to persons with actual notice, and as to others upon filing with the Division of the Federal Register. Retroactive rules are not precluded if otherwise legal and accompanied by the required finding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Section 4(c) does not supersede statutes requiring longer effective-notice periods
rubrics_metrics.description: Section 4(c) is not intended to repeal other statutes which require a period longer than thirty days between issuance and the effective date of certain rules (e.g., Cotton Standards Act requires one-year period).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When another statute prescribes a longer delay, that statute controls over the 30-day rule in section 4(c).

rubrics_metrics.name: If agency omits section 4(a)/(b) procedures for impracticability, still must include 4(c) finding to dispense with 30 days
rubrics_metrics.description: Where an agency omits the procedures of section 4(a) and (b) because 'notice and public procedure thereon are impracticable, unnecessary or contrary to the public interest', subsection (c) does not thereby become automatically inoperative; if dispensing with the thirty‑day provision is also compelled, the rule should contain the finding required by the last clause of section 4(c).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Agencies must make the separate finding and publish it with the rule if they are also dispensing with the 30-day lead time.

rubrics_metrics.name: Section 4(d) — right to petition for issuance, amendment, or repeal
rubrics_metrics.description: Every agency shall accord any interested person the right to petition for the issuance, amendment, or repeal of a rule. Applies to substantive rules, interpretations, statements of general policy, organizational and procedural rules, and to existing and proposed rules.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The right may be reasonably limited to persons whose interests are or will be affected. The mere filing of a petition does not require the agency to grant it, hold a hearing, or engage in public rulemaking proceedings; special statutory schemes (e.g., FDCA §701(e)) may condition hearings on petitions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Publish procedural rules for petitions (section 3(a)(2))
rubrics_metrics.description: Every agency with rulemaking powers subject to section 4 should establish and publish procedural rules governing the receipt, consideration and disposition of petitions filed pursuant to section 4(d).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Procedural rules may call for: a statement of the rulemaking action sought, any supporting data, a declaration of the petitioner's interest, and compliance with reasonable formal requirements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Agency action on petitions and denial — notice and nonreviewability
rubrics_metrics.description: The agency need act on the petition only in accordance with its published procedures. The denial of a petition is governed by section 6(d); prompt notice of such denial should be given to the petitioner with a simple statement of the procedural or other grounds. Neither denial of a petition nor refusal to hold public rulemaking proceedings is subject to judicial review.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Agencies should provide prompt and simple reasons for denial in accordance with their procedures, but petition denial is not judicially reviewable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Section 5 — scope: formal procedural requirements apply only where statute requires adjudication 'on the record after opportunity for an agency hearing'
rubrics_metrics.description: Sections 5, 7 and 8 govern formal administrative adjudication but are invoked only where agency action 'on the record after opportunity for an agency hearing' is required by some other statute.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The word 'statute' was used deliberately: mere authorization to hold hearings (e.g., 'such hearings as may be deemed necessary') does not trigger sections 5, 7, and 8. If a hearing is held but not required by statute, those formal requirements do not apply.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of 'adjudication' and 'order'
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Adjudication' is defined as 'agency process for the formulation of an order'; 'order' is defined as 'the whole or any part of the final disposition (whether affirmative, negative, injunctive, or declaratory in form) of any agency in any matter other than rule making but including licensing' (section 2(d)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Investigatory proceedings that do not lead to issuance of an order are not adjudications. Some administrative functions (e.g., loan administration) traditionally are not adjudicatory unless defined as such by statute.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exemption 1 — matters subject to trial de novo in court
rubrics_metrics.description: Any matter subject to a subsequent trial of the law and the facts de novo in any court is exempt from the provisions of section 5 (and therefore sections 7 and 8).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where agency adjudication is only prima facie and the aggrieved party is entitled to a complete judicial retrial, formal administrative procedures are unnecessary. Examples include certain reparation orders.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exemption 2 — selection or tenure of officers/employees (except examiners)
rubrics_metrics.description: The selection or tenure of an officer or employee of the United States other than examiners appointed pursuant to section 11 is exempt from the formal procedural requirements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Selection and control of public personnel traditionally are discretionary. Proceedings for removal of 'examiners' under section 11 are not exempt and must follow sections 6, 7 and 8.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exemption 3 — proceedings resting 'solely' on inspections, tests, or elections
rubrics_metrics.description: Proceedings in which decisions 'rest solely on inspections, tests, or elections' are exempt because such determinations do not lend themselves to the hearing process.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applies even if statute provides for a hearing; 'rest solely' means issues are determined mainly by inspection/test/election. Examples: denial of airman certificates, local seaworthiness certificates, locomotive inspections, grading of grain. Formal hearings would add little protection and could hinder necessary prompt decisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exemption 4 — military, naval, or foreign affairs functions
rubrics_metrics.description: The conduct of military, naval, or foreign affairs functions is exempt from the provisions of section 5.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such functions are exempt for reasons similar to exemptions in section 1 and typically do not involve statutory requirements for hearings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exemption 5 — cases where agency acts as agent for a court
rubrics_metrics.description: Proceedings in which an agency is acting as an agent for a court are exempt from section 5.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These are procedural/ministerial functions performed for a court; exempt because court control of process and review differs from agency adjudication.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exemption 6 — certification of employee representatives
rubrics_metrics.description: The certification of employee representatives (e.g., Labor Board operations under NLRA §9(c) and National Mediation Board certification under the Railway Labor Act) is exempt because such determinations rest largely upon an election or the availability of an election.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Included because certification decisions resemble elections and do not require full formal adjudicatory procedures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Section 5(a)(1) — notice of time, place, and nature of hearing
rubrics_metrics.description: Persons entitled to notice of an agency hearing shall be timely informed of the time, place, and nature thereof.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The subsection requires 'timely' notice; what is timely depends on circumstances (urgency, complexity). Nothing in this subsection overrides other statutes prescribing specific notice periods (e.g., 30 days under FTC Act). Notice should specify the nature of the hearing (e.g., whether a cease-and-desist order may issue). When fixing times/places, agencies must give due regard to convenience and necessity of parties consistent with public interest.

rubrics_metrics.name: Section 5(a)(2) — notice of legal authority and jurisdiction
rubrics_metrics.description: Notice must inform parties of 'the legal authority and jurisdiction under which the hearing is to be held'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The notice should reference the agency's authority sufficiently to enable parties to identify and raise relevant legal issues.
